title: Pano AI cameras on Xcel and CORE Electric towers spot the Bear Creek Fire; helicopters hold it to three acres
summary: Utility-funded Pano AI cameras detected smoke from the 16 June 2024 Bear Creek Fire in Douglas County, Colorado; helicopters were dispatched within 30 minutes and the fire was held to three acres.
account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The original joint utility statement specifies 5.5 hours of helicopter operations, 17,765 gallons of water, and containment at three acres by 7 p.m. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein). The OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a separate positively framed record of Xcel's November 2023 Pano AI deployment.
purpose: Pano AI cameras rotate 360 degrees on mountaintop towers and use AI to detect smoke plumes. They alert utilities and fire agencies with a triangulated location. Detecting this fire early was the intended use.
system: Pano AI wildfire detection cameras (Pano Rapid Detect)
deployer: Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative
taxonomy_note: Fire spread averted is read as reduced potential for harm; Trustible's description stresses legal harm.

ratings.reason: The fire was held to three acres after helicopters were dispatched within 30 minutes. CORE's CEO called the detection and location “crucial”. Simultaneous Forest Service identification limits what can be attributed to the cameras.
CORE Electric and Xcel Energy obtained a fast, located alert supporting their wildfire mitigation strategy. Denver7 quotes CORE's Jordan Ambrogi saying alerts typically beat 911 calls.
No individual beneficiary is documented in the sources.

ai_role.statement: The AI smoke detection supplied an alert and location. CORE’s original joint utility account states that the cameras identified the fire simultaneously with the U.S. Forest Service. The account describes how the coordinates assisted the response, but does not establish the AI’s incremental contribution to the three-acre outcome.

fields.account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The original joint utility statement specifies 5.5 hours of helicopter operations, 17,765 gallons of water, and containment at three acres by 7 p.m. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein). The OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a separate positively framed record of Xcel's November 2023 Pano AI deployment.

fields.headline: Pano AI cameras spot the Bear Creek Fire; held to three acres

Deterministic content version assigned by the local migration.

fields.account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The original joint utility statement specifies 5.5 hours of helicopter operations, 17,765 gallons of water, and containment at three acres by 7 p.m. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein). The OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a separate positively framed record of Xcel's November 2023 Pano AI deployment.

produced_by: Camera stations with 360-degree views sited on cell towers within roughly 10 miles of the ignition
Alert routing to both the utility and local fire agencies with a triangulated location
Lightning-caused ignition in daylight in a remote area, with aerial resources available for dispatch
must_hold: Camera coverage of the ignition point and functioning AI smoke detection
An agency able to act on the alert within minutes
Independent confirmation of who detected the fire first, since the utilities report simultaneous Forest Service identification
